content.content:
---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/donetick/donetick
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: donetick/donetick:v0.1.76
  port: 2021
  vm: m1.small
  flavor_id: "2"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0348
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: donetick
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ THE CONTAINER REFUSES TO START UNTIL YOU SET DT_JWT_SECRET, AND THIS IS THE ONE THAT WOULD OTHERWISE EAT YOUR EVENING. Dockerfile:43 copies the repo's config directory INTO the image, so /config/selfhosted.yaml ships with jwt.secret set to the placeholder string change_this_to_a_secure_random_string_32_characters_long. config/config.go:404-446 puts that exact string in a weakSecrets list and PANICS the process when it matches, or when the secret is shorter than 32 characters. The log prints a SECURITY ERROR block, suggests a generated secret, and aborts. So a deploy that passes no environment at all produces a crash-looping container and a redu build that never goes healthy, and the cause is a config file you never wrote. Generate 32 or more random alphanumeric characters and pass DT_JWT_SECRET. This is fail-loud rather than fail-silent, which is the good version of this trap, but only if you know why."
  - "PASS THE SAME DT_JWT_SECRET ON EVERY REDEPLOY. It signs every session token (jwt.session_time defaults to 168h in the shipped config, max_refresh 1440h), so a new value on each deploy silently logs every user out, including the mobile app and any long-lived API token flow that rides on it. Nothing errors. Generate it ONCE, hand it to the user, and reuse it forever. It is not a database key, so rotating it destroys no data; it destroys sessions."
  - "⛔⛔ DATABASE: SET DT_DATABASE_TYPE=postgres EXACTLY, BECAUSE ANYTHING ELSE SILENTLY MEANS SQLITE. internal/database/database.go:59-77 is a switch with ONE case, \"postgres\", and a default branch that opens SQLite. A typo, the string postgresql, or an override that did not take all land in the default branch, so the app comes up perfectly healthy, serves the UI, saves your chores, and loses all of them at the next VM replacement (the file is $DT_SQLITE_PATH, or ./donetick.db relative to /, when that is unset). Set ALL of: DT_DATABASE_TYPE=postgres, DT_DATABASE_HOST=${PGHOST}, DT_DATABASE_PORT=${PGPORT}, DT_DATABASE_USER=${PGUSER}, DT_DATABASE_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value]}, DT_DATABASE_NAME=${PGDATABASE}. deploy_compose with database:'managed' only APPENDS those PG variables to the project .env; it never edits your compose, so the compose has to interpolate them itself. Environment variables beat the baked config file: config/config.go:350-352 sets the DT prefix and replaces dots with underscores, then AutomaticEnv applies them over the file."
  - "⛔ PROVE WHICH DATABASE IT LANDED IN, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, BECAUSE A GREEN PAGE PROVES NOTHING HERE. POSITIVE, and run it first because it also proves your exec command works at all: `sudo docker exec <container> printenv DT_DATABASE_TYPE DT_DATABASE_HOST` must print postgres and the managed private IP. POSITIVE, and this is the one that settles it: connect to the managed Postgres and confirm Donetick's tables are there (the migrations create users, circles and chores among others, and the startup log prints 'Applied N migrations!'). NEGATIVE, and only meaningful next to those two: `sudo docker exec <container> ls -la /donetick.db` should not find a file. The runtime image is alpine, so it has a shell and exec really works, unlike the distroless entries elsewhere in this library."
  - "THE POSTGRES CONNECTION IS UNENCRYPTED AND YOU CANNOT CHANGE IT FROM CONFIG. internal/database/database.go:61 builds the DSN with sslmode=disable and TimeZone=Asia/Shanghai written into the format string, with no configuration hook for either. Over redu's private network, where the managed database VM is not reachable from the internet, plaintext is survivable, and it is still worth saying out loud at handover rather than letting the user assume TLS. The hardcoded time zone applies to the database session; set the container's own TZ variable for the application's clock, which is what drives due dates and the scheduler."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: NOBODY, AND THAT IS AN UNUSUAL ANSWER WORTH READING TWICE. Donetick has no instance administrator and no first-user privilege. internal/user/handler.go:175-195: every account that signs up gets its OWN circle (its household) and is given the admin role INSIDE THAT CIRCLE ONLY. A stranger who signs up on your instance therefore cannot see your chores, but they do get an account, a circle, storage and scheduler work on the VM you are paying for, and there is no admin UI anywhere to remove them: deleting them means SQL against the managed database. The ONLY instance-level control is closing signups, described next. The dashboard-view and admin/manager roles named in the README are also circle roles, resolved from OIDC groups (internal/auth/role_resolver.go), not instance roles."
  - "⛔ CLOSE SIGNUPS, AND DO IT AFTER YOU HAVE CREATED YOUR OWN ACCOUNT. The shipped config has is_user_creation_disabled: false, so registration is open to anyone the moment the hostname resolves. Two switches do the same thing: DT_IS_USER_CREATION_DISABLED=true through the normal viper path, and DONETICK_DISABLE_SIGNUP=true, which is the ONE variable in this app that does NOT use the DT_ prefix (config/config.go:317). Set it and internal/user/handler.go:115-120 answers 403 'User creation is disabled' to POST /api/v1/auth/ before it even parses the body. Order matters: create the household's accounts first, then close the door and redeploy. There is no invite system to let people in afterwards, so reopening means another redeploy."
  - "⛔ DT_SINGLE_CIRCLE_INSTANCE=true CHANGES WHO LANDS IN YOUR HOUSEHOLD. It hides the circle-management UI and puts new OIDC users into the SHARED circle (ID 1) instead of giving them their own, which is what makes a family instance pleasant. It also means that anyone your identity provider lets in is inside your task list rather than beside it. Only enable it together with an identity provider whose membership you control, and pair it with DT_DISABLE_PASSWORD_AUTH=[REDACTED:value] so password signup is not a second, ungoverned door."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH: the frontend, GET /health (which returns status, version and commit, internal/resource/handler.go:53-63), GET /api/v1/health (bodyless 200, main.go:341-343), and GET /api/v1/resource, which is unauthenticated and reports is_user_creation_disabled, single_circle_instance, disable_password_auth, the API version and the configured OIDC client id and auth URL. That last one is genuinely useful for verification and it is also a fingerprint, so treat the version it publishes as public information. Everything else is behind the JWT middleware. The shipped config also has serve_swagger true, which publishes the API documentation at /swagger/index.html: harmless, and set server.serve_swagger false if the user would rather not advertise the surface."
  - "⛔ PIN donetick/donetick:v0.1.76 WITH THE v, AND KNOW WHAT THE RELEASE FEED LOOKS LIKE. Measured against the Docker Hub API on 2026-08-17: the v0.1.76 tag exists (pushed 2026-07-26) and the same version WITHOUT the v returns 404. v0.1.76 is the newest NON-prerelease release; the five newest GitHub releases are all betas, and a rolling `beta` tag on Docker Hub tracks them. This project ships beta tags frequently, so pinning matters more here than usual: take the newest stable tag deliberately rather than following latest."
  - "⛔ DO NOT ADAPT THE REPO'S docker-compose.yaml. It is wrong for the published image in three separate ways: it builds from the Dockerfile instead of pulling, it publishes 8085:8000 when the server listens on 2021 (config/selfhosted.yaml:22, Dockerfile:50), and it overrides the command with /donetick-core, which does not exist in the image (Dockerfile:33 and :42 build and copy /donetick). Copy the compose from the README instead, which is correct, then drop its SQLite volume and DT_SQLITE_PATH once the managed Postgres is wired."
  - "PORT 2021, AND THERE ARE TWO HEALTH ENDPOINTS WITH DIFFERENT BODIES. Pass 2021 to deploy_compose. Dockerfile:52-53 defines a container HEALTHCHECK using wget against /health, which the alpine image has (there is no curl in it, so a curl-based healthcheck silently never succeeds). For your own probing prefer GET /health, because it returns a JSON body with status, version and commit and can therefore prove you are talking to Donetick, while /api/v1/health returns a bare 200 that an error page could imitate."
  - "SET DT_SERVER_PUBLIC_HOST TO THE REAL HTTPS URL. It defaults to http://localhost:2021 (config/config.go:137) and it feeds generated links, including the Swagger host and the password-reset URL. Generate the dname yourself in full `donetick-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud` form so the value is known before the container starts, and set it as https://<that>, with no trailing slash. If the user will also use the mobile app or any other cross-origin client, the shipped cors_allow_origins list contains only localhost entries, and it is a list, so it is easier to override by mounting your own selfhosted.yaml than through the environment."
  - "NO SMTP MEANS NO PASSWORD RESET BY EMAIL, AND THE SHIPPED CONFIG SAYS SO. The email block in config/selfhosted.yaml is empty and carries log_raw_url: true, which logs the password-reset URL to the console when mail is not configured. So a lost password on a fresh instance is recovered by reading the container log, which is fine for a household and worth stating at handover. Point the email block at a relay the user already owns if they want real resets, and remember the app also speaks Telegram, Discord and Pushover for notifications, none of which needs SMTP."
  - "PHOTO ATTACHMENTS DEFAULT TO S3, NOT TO LOCAL DISK, WHICH SURPRISES PEOPLE. internal/storage/factory.go:10-17: storage_type \"local\" uses the filesystem and ANYTHING else, including the empty default in the shipped config, constructs an S3 client. Building it does not fail with empty credentials, so the app starts happily and the problem only appears when somebody attaches a photo. If the user wants photos: either set the storage block to local with a base_path inside a mounted volume, or give it real S3-compatible credentials (bucket, region, endpoint, access key, secret key). If they do not, nothing is broken, that feature is simply unused."
  - "NO VOLUME IS NEEDED ONCE POSTGRES IS WIRED, WITH ONE EXCEPTION. Chores, circles, users and history all live in the managed database. The /donetick-data volume in upstream's compose exists only for the SQLite file this recipe deliberately does not use, so mounting it and assuming it protects something is a mistake. The exception is local photo storage: if you enable it, mount a volume and put the base_path inside it, and say plainly that those files live on the app VM and go with it."
  - "NO migrate_command. config/selfhosted.yaml:10 sets database.migration true and main.go:279-280 runs the migrations at startup, printing 'Applied N migrations!'. A fresh managed Postgres is therefore populated on first boot and an upgrade applies its own migrations. Donetick needs exactly ONE database and creates no second one, so redu's one-database-per-managed-server rule never bites, and no db_superuser is needed."
  - "SIZING IS REASONING, NOT A MEASUREMENT. Upstream publishes no memory figure anywhere (checked README, Dockerfile, their compose and the shipped config). m1.small (1 vCPU / 2 GB) is chosen because this is one statically linked Go binary with the frontend embedded in it, running on alpine, with the database on a separate VM. The scheduler jobs (due, overdue and pre-due, every 30m to 3h in the shipped config) and the realtime SSE service (1000 connections allowed by default) are the only background load. SOURCE IS EITHER GIT OR UPLOAD, NEVER BOTH. For code that is not pushed, or is private, or needs fixing first: write the files locally, call prepare_upload, run the tar+curl block it returns, then pass the source_token and NO repo. ⚠️ prepare_upload EXCLUDES .env from the tarball by design, so secrets have to reach the VM another way (pass them to the deploy call, not in the tree).

Call delete_database too, and say so to the user before either.

A MANAGED POSTGRES SERVES EXACTLY ONE DATABASE. pg_hba is evaluated before role privileges, so being superuser does not help. An app that wants a second database needs a second managed server. This has broken deploys that otherwise looked healthy.

get_deployment RETURNS THE MERGED redu.md ONLY WHEN IT FITS ITS RESPONSE BUDGET. Over budget - which is normal for a mature recipe or any large app - it withholds redu_md_markdown and returns redu_md_last_deploy_block plus redu_md_deploy_log_line instead. That is NOT an error and must not be retried: apply those two edits to the file on disk and change nothing else.

⛔ THE MERGE NEVER WRITES A NEW QUIRK. Whatever redu returns, it refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Every gotcha YOUR run discovered has to be typed into the quirks list by hand before you commit, or it is lost - and that list is the only part of the file that makes the next deploy cheaper.
⛔ NEVER WRITE A CREDENTIAL INTO redu.md. It is committed and read by the next person and the next agent. Names of variables, yes; their values, never. Hand secrets to the user in the session instead.

plan_deploy OVER-SIZES A PULLED COMPOSE STACK. Measured 8 times out of 8: declaring needs_compose makes it quote m1.large, roughly double the real requirement, because it cannot see that the images are pulled rather than built. Show the user the plan, but size from the app's real memory figure when you have one.

THE MANAGED DATABASE PASSWORD IS ON THE VM, NOT IN THE API. list_databases returns private_ip, port, db_name and db_user and DELIBERATELY NOT the password, so an agent that looks for it there finds nothing and starts guessing. The deploy writes the whole connection set into the compose project's .env on the app VM. Call get_env_keys for the NAMES first (no SSH, values never leave the VM); only if you need an actual VALUE, SSH in (get_ssh_command) and read that one key, `sudo grep '^PGPASSWORD=' /opt/app-src/.env`. ⚠️ That file is chmod 600 root:root so it needs sudo, and the database is on the PRIVATE network - reachable from the app VM, never from a laptop.

YOU CAN READ A DEPLOY VM WITHOUT SSHING INTO IT, and four tools do it: get_containers (what is running, health, restarts, crashed ones included), get_container_logs (what the app actually printed - the tool for 'deployed fine but does not work'), get_resource_usage (memory, disk, load, OOM kills) and get_env_keys (which variables got wired, by name). ⛔ get_instance_logs is the SERIAL CONSOLE and is not your app's logs; build_log stops when the build does. SSH is still yours for everything else - a shell on a real machine is the point, not a fallback.

⛔ THE PRIMARY SURFACE'S HOSTNAME COMES FROM THE TOP-LEVEL dname, NOT FROM expose[0].dname, WHICH IS SILENTLY DISCARDED. Extra expose entries DO keep the dname you give them, so the two behave differently and nothing tells you. If an app bakes its own public URL into config at boot (CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN, allowed_origins, SITE_URL), generate the full `<label>-<8 lowercase letters/digits>.redu.cloud` form yourself and pass it as the TOP-LEVEL dname, which is used verbatim. Passing it on expose[0] instead gets you an app configured for a hostname redu never created, answering 200 on a name it does not believe is its own.

WEBSOCKETS WORK THROUGH THE PROXY WITH NO CONFIGURATION: every proxy host redu creates has upgrade enabled. Measured at the protocol level, HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with the subprotocol echoed back. ⚠️ TEST IT WITH `curl --http1.1`: plain curl negotiates HTTP/2, which has no Upgrade mechanism at all, so the app answers as an ordinary GET and the failure looks exactly like a proxy refusing to upgrade. Browsers use HTTP/1.1 for websockets regardless. Do not disable an app's realtime features on the strength of an HTTP/2 curl.

---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/donetick/donetick
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: donetick/donetick:v0.1.76
  port: 2021
  vm: m1.small
  flavor_id: "2"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0348
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: donetick
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ THE CONTAINER REFUSES TO START UNTIL YOU SET DT_JWT_SECRET, AND THIS IS THE ONE THAT WOULD OTHERWISE EAT YOUR EVENING. Dockerfile:43 copies the repo's config directory INTO the image, so /config/selfhosted.yaml ships with jwt.secret set to the placeholder string change_this_to_a_secure_random_string_32_characters_long. config/config.go:404-446 puts that exact string in a weakSecrets list and PANICS the process when it matches, or when the secret is shorter than 32 characters. The log prints a SECURITY ERROR block, suggests a generated secret, and aborts. So a deploy that passes no environment at all produces a crash-looping container and a redu build that never goes healthy, and the cause is a config file you never wrote. Generate 32 or more random alphanumeric characters and pass DT_JWT_SECRET. This is fail-loud rather than fail-silent, which is the good version of this trap, but only if you know why."
  - "PASS THE SAME DT_JWT_SECRET ON EVERY REDEPLOY. It signs every session token (jwt.session_time defaults to 168h in the shipped config, max_refresh 1440h), so a new value on each deploy silently logs every user out, including the mobile app and any long-lived API token flow that rides on it. Nothing errors. Generate it ONCE, hand it to the user, and reuse it forever. It is not a database key, so rotating it destroys no data; it destroys sessions."
  - "⛔⛔ DATABASE: SET DT_DATABASE_TYPE=postgres EXACTLY, BECAUSE ANYTHING ELSE SILENTLY MEANS SQLITE. internal/database/database.go:59-77 is a switch with ONE case, \"postgres\", and a default branch that opens SQLite. A typo, the string postgresql, or an override that did not take all land in the default branch, so the app comes up perfectly healthy, serves the UI, saves your chores, and loses all of them at the next VM replacement (the file is $DT_SQLITE_PATH, or ./donetick.db relative to /, when that is unset). Set ALL of: DT_DATABASE_TYPE=postgres, DT_DATABASE_HOST=${PGHOST}, DT_DATABASE_PORT=${PGPORT}, DT_DATABASE_USER=${PGUSER}, DT_DATABASE_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value]}, DT_DATABASE_NAME=${PGDATABASE}. deploy_compose with database:'managed' only APPENDS those PG variables to the project .env; it never edits your compose, so the compose has to interpolate them itself. Environment variables beat the baked config file: config/config.go:350-352 sets the DT prefix and replaces dots with underscores, then AutomaticEnv applies them over the file."
  - "⛔ PROVE WHICH DATABASE IT LANDED IN, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, BECAUSE A GREEN PAGE PROVES NOTHING HERE. POSITIVE, and run it first because it also proves your exec command works at all: `sudo docker exec <container> printenv DT_DATABASE_TYPE DT_DATABASE_HOST` must print postgres and the managed private IP. POSITIVE, and this is the one that settles it: connect to the managed Postgres and confirm Donetick's tables are there (the migrations create users, circles and chores among others, and the startup log prints 'Applied N migrations!'). NEGATIVE, and only meaningful next to those two: `sudo docker exec <container> ls -la /donetick.db` should not find a file. The runtime image is alpine, so it has a shell and exec really works, unlike the distroless entries elsewhere in this library."
  - "THE POSTGRES CONNECTION IS UNENCRYPTED AND YOU CANNOT CHANGE IT FROM CONFIG. internal/database/database.go:61 builds the DSN with sslmode=disable and TimeZone=Asia/Shanghai written into the format string, with no configuration hook for either. Over redu's private network, where the managed database VM is not reachable from the internet, plaintext is survivable, and it is still worth saying out loud at handover rather than letting the user assume TLS. The hardcoded time zone applies to the database session; set the container's own TZ variable for the application's clock, which is what drives due dates and the scheduler."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: NOBODY, AND THAT IS AN UNUSUAL ANSWER WORTH READING TWICE. Donetick has no instance administrator and no first-user privilege. internal/user/handler.go:175-195: every account that signs up gets its OWN circle (its household) and is given the admin role INSIDE THAT CIRCLE ONLY. A stranger who signs up on your instance therefore cannot see your chores, but they do get an account, a circle, storage and scheduler work on the VM you are paying for, and there is no admin UI anywhere to remove them: deleting them means SQL against the managed database. The ONLY instance-level control is closing signups, described next. The dashboard-view and admin/manager roles named in the README are also circle roles, resolved from OIDC groups (internal/auth/role_resolver.go), not instance roles."
  - "⛔ CLOSE SIGNUPS, AND DO IT AFTER YOU HAVE CREATED YOUR OWN ACCOUNT. The shipped config has is_user_creation_disabled: false, so registration is open to anyone the moment the hostname resolves. Two switches do the same thing: DT_IS_USER_CREATION_DISABLED=true through the normal viper path, and DONETICK_DISABLE_SIGNUP=true, which is the ONE variable in this app that does NOT use the DT_ prefix (config/config.go:317). Set it and internal/user/handler.go:115-120 answers 403 'User creation is disabled' to POST /api/v1/auth/ before it even parses the body. Order matters: create the household's accounts first, then close the door and redeploy. There is no invite system to let people in afterwards, so reopening means another redeploy."
  - "⛔ DT_SINGLE_CIRCLE_INSTANCE=true CHANGES WHO LANDS IN YOUR HOUSEHOLD. It hides the circle-management UI and puts new OIDC users into the SHARED circle (ID 1) instead of giving them their own, which is what makes a family instance pleasant. It also means that anyone your identity provider lets in is inside your task list rather than beside it. Only enable it together with an identity provider whose membership you control, and pair it with DT_DISABLE_PASSWORD_AUTH=[REDACTED:value] so password signup is not a second, ungoverned door."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH: the frontend, GET /health (which returns status, version and commit, internal/resource/handler.go:53-63), GET /api/v1/health (bodyless 200, main.go:341-343), and GET /api/v1/resource, which is unauthenticated and reports is_user_creation_disabled, single_circle_instance, disable_password_auth, the API version and the configured OIDC client id and auth URL. That last one is genuinely useful for verification and it is also a fingerprint, so treat the version it publishes as public information. Everything else is behind the JWT middleware. The shipped config also has serve_swagger true, which publishes the API documentation at /swagger/index.html: harmless, and set server.serve_swagger false if the user would rather not advertise the surface."
  - "⛔ PIN donetick/donetick:v0.1.76 WITH THE v, AND KNOW WHAT THE RELEASE FEED LOOKS LIKE. Measured against the Docker Hub API on 2026-08-17: the v0.1.76 tag exists (pushed 2026-07-26) and the same version WITHOUT the v returns 404. v0.1.76 is the newest NON-prerelease release; the five newest GitHub releases are all betas, and a rolling `beta` tag on Docker Hub tracks them. # Self-host Donetick on redu

Chores and recurring tasks for a household or a person, with scheduling that actually understands
"every other Tuesday", assignee rotation, subtasks, labels and points. One small Go container, a
managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS URL.

About GBP 0.035/hour, roughly GBP 25 a month. Inside the no-card free trial.

## What this deploys

- **Donetick** from the official image, pinned to `v0.1.76`, on one m1.small VM, port 2021.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, holding every chore, circle and completion.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

No volume: with Postgres wired there is nothing durable left on the app VM, unless you turn on
local photo attachments.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Donetick on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## One decision to make before you deploy

**Who is allowed to make an account?** Donetick has no instance administrator: every person who
signs up gets their own circle, and there is no admin screen anywhere to remove them afterwards.

- **Personal or household instance**: create your accounts during the deploy, then set
  `DONETICK_DISABLE_SIGNUP=true` and redeploy. There is no invite system, so adding somebody
  later means opening signups again briefly.
- **Open instance**: leave it open, and understand that strangers will have accounts on a VM you
  pay for. They cannot see your tasks, since circles are separate.

## The three that actually break it

**The image will not start with its own config.** The published image contains
`config/selfhosted.yaml` with a placeholder JWT secret, and the app has that exact string on a
blocklist and panics. Pass `DT_JWT_SECRET` with 32 or more random characters or the container
crash-loops with a "SECURITY ERROR" banner and the build never goes healthy.

**Anything other than the exact string `postgres` means SQLite.** The database selector is a
switch with one case and a default branch that opens a local file. It comes up healthy either way,
and one of the two loses your chores at the next redeploy.

**Their `docker-compose.yaml` is wrong for the published image.** It builds from source, exposes
the wrong port, and runs a binary name that does not exist in the image. Use the compose from the
README instead.

## Verify it after boot

Run this from your machine. It refuses to pass when it cannot tell.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# HOST=donetick-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud ./verify.sh
set -u
: "${HOST:?set HOST to the public hostname}"

body=$(mktemp)
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$body" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/health")

if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "503" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the edge answered $code, which is what redu serves while a container is"
  echo "still starting. It is also what you get from a container that is crash-looping on a weak"
  echo "JWT secret, so if this persists, read the container log before re-running."
  rm -f "$body"; exit 2
fi
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "FAIL: /health answered $code"; rm -f "$body"; exit 1; }

# Positive control FIRST: Donetick's own health document. Without this match every assertion
# below is meaningless, because an error page can also return a 200 in some proxy setups.
grep -q '"status":"healthy"' "$body" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: HTTP 200 but the body is not Donetick's health JSON."
  rm -f "$body"; exit 2; }
rm -f "$body"

# Read the flag the instance reports about itself.
flag=$(curl -sSL "https://$HOST/api/v1/resource")
echo "$flag" | grep -q 'is_user_creation_disabled' || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/v1/resource did not answer with the expected fields."; exit 2; }

# Now TEST THE BEHAVIOUR, not the flag. An empty body is rejected at 400 by the parser when
# signup is open, and at 403 BEFORE the body is parsed when it is closed, so this probes the
# door without ever creating an account.
sig=$(printf '{}' | curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
        -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @- \
        "https://$HOST/api/v1/auth/")
case "$sig" in
  403) echo "OK: signup is CLOSED (403 before the body is parsed)" ;;
  400) echo "NOTE: signup is OPEN. Anyone with this URL can create an account and their own"
       echo "circle. Expected while you are still creating the household's accounts; set"
       echo "DONETICK_DISABLE_SIGNUP=true and redeploy once you are done." ;;
  404) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the signup route answered 404, so it has moved and this check proves"
       echo "nothing. Find the current route before trusting anything here."; exit 2 ;;
  *)   echo "INCONCLUSIVE: signup probe answered $sig, which is neither 400 nor 403."; exit 2 ;;
esac

echo
echo "Still to confirm, and it cannot be seen from out here: WHICH database."
echo "  sudo docker exec <container> printenv DT_DATABASE_TYPE DT_DATABASE_HOST"
echo "  must print postgres and the managed private IP, and Donetick's tables must exist in"
echo "  the managed Postgres. A healthy page proves nothing about that."
```
